subtitle: The tools every later chapter uses: Ohm, Kirchhoff, dividers, LED, RC
takeaways: Every connection is a divider: watch the load
Size LED resistors from V_{S} − V_{F}, round up
τ = RC: 63 % after τ, settled after 5τ

slides.title: Ohm's law, power and standard values
bullets: Calculate in V, kΩ and mA: no powers of ten needed
P = V·I = I^{2}R = V^{2}/R; stay below about 50 % of the power rating
Capstone: sensor current limited to 1 mA because of self-heating
slides.notes: Quick repetition from the intro course. Stress the kΩ/mA/V habit and the 50 % power rule; 100 Ω at 5 V already dissipates 250 mW. A design always ends with picking the next E-series value and recalculating.

slides.title: Series and parallel

left.head: Series
bullets: Same current, voltages add (KVL)
Larger than the largest resistor

right.head: Parallel
bullets: Same voltage, currents add (KCL)
Smaller than the smallest; R‖R = R/2

slides.notes: KCL: charge is not lost at a node; KVL: the voltages around a loop sum to zero. For our small networks we just combine series and parallel step by step.

slides.title: Falstad: series-parallel network

falstad.name: network
falstad.hint: Hover over each resistor: current and power; check KCL at node A

observe: Recipe: combine parallel, add series, total current, then go back
KCL at node A as a cheap check: I_{1} = I_{2} + I_{3}
Compare each resistor's power with a 0.25 W rating
slides.notes: 12 V, 100 Ω, 220 Ω ‖ 330 Ω; V_{A} = 6.83 V. Exercise 1.1 finds that R_{1} is overloaded and R_{2} runs too hot for the 50 % rule.

slides.title: The voltage divider and its load
bullets: Unloaded: the voltages divide in the ratio of the resistances
Seen from the load: V_{th} = V_{0}·R_{2}/(R_{1}+R_{2}), R_{th} = R_{1}‖R_{2}
R_{L} ≥ 10·R_{th} for < 10 % error, ≥ 100·R_{th} for < 1 % (or buffer it)
Small R: stiff but high cross current; large R: sensitive to every load
Capstone ADC ladder: 8 × 1 kΩ at 4 V, loaded only by comparator inputs

falstad.name: divider_loaded
falstad.hint: Compare Vout_open (5.00 V) and Vout_load (3.33 V)

slides.notes: The divider is the most used circuit in the lecture. In the example 10 kΩ/10 kΩ loaded with 10 kΩ loses one third of the output (Exercise 1.2). A trimmer between two fixed resistors gives a fine adjustment; in the capstone it sets the gain for exactly 0 … 4.00 V.

slides.title: Current divider
bullets: The smaller resistor takes the larger current
Potentiometer wiper: V_{out} = x·V_{0}; load the wiper only lightly

falstad.name: current_divider
falstad.hint: 10 mA into 1 kΩ ‖ 4.7 kΩ: read 8.25 mA and 1.75 mA

slides.notes: The current divider is the dual of the voltage divider. Mention potentiometers and trimmers briefly here; the slide 'Potentiometer: adjustable divider' in the script has the details.

slides.title: Thevenin equivalent and load line
bullets: Any linear two-terminal network = V_{th} in series with R_{th}
V_{th} = V_{oc}, R_{th} = V_{oc}/I_{sc}, or set sources to zero
Zeroed sources: voltage source → wire, current source → open
Operating point: source line V_{th} − R_{th}·I_{L} meets the load line

falstad.name: thevenin
falstad.hint: VL_orig = VL_equiv = 3.10 V; short R_{L} to read I_{sc}

slides.notes: The example is the 12 V divider 2.2 kΩ/3.3 kΩ with a 1 kΩ load: 7.2 V behind 1.32 kΩ. The load line also works for nonlinear loads like LEDs. Derivation in Exercise 1.3.

slides.title: Falstad: superposition

falstad.name: superposition
falstad.hint: Read VX1, VX2 and VX: 6.00 V + 1.25 V = 7.25 V

observe: Each source alone, the other set to zero, then add the results
Only for linear circuits: fails when a diode switches or an op-amp clips
Not valid for power (quadratic in current)
slides.notes: Superposition comes back for summing amplifiers and offset voltages. Exercise 1.4 checks the result with KCL and shows that the 5 V source is being charged.

slides.title: The LED: a nonlinear load
bullets: Current rises exponentially: never connect an LED directly to a source
Model: constant V_{F}; red ≈ 2.0 V, green/blue/white (InGaN) ≈ 3.0 V
Standard LEDs ≤ 20 mA; modern ones are visible at 2 … 5 mA
Reverse voltage only about 5 V: an LED is not a rectifier
slides.notes: V_{F} grows with photon energy. A blue LED on 3.3 V leaves only a few hundred mV for the resistor. V_{F} drops by about 2 mV/K, so an LED without resistor runs away thermally.

slides.title: Design recipe: LED series resistor
steps: Take V_{F} from the datasheet at the desired current (red 2.0 V, blue 3.0 V)
Choose I_{F}: 2 … 10 mA for an indicator; check the driver's maximum
R = (V_{S} − V_{F})/I_{F}, round up to the next E12/E24 value
Recalculate I_{F}, check P_{R} = I_{F}^{2}·R against the rating
slides.notes: Rounding up protects LED and driver. The larger V_{S} − V_{F}, the less the current depends on the spread of V_{F}. Example: 5 V, red LED, 10 mA gives 330 Ω and 9.1 mA.

slides.title: Falstad: LED on a logic output

falstad.name: led_resistor
falstad.hint: Read VLED (1.78 V), move the R slider, watch the blinking pair

observe: Source (LED to ground, on at high) or sink (LED to supply, on at low)
74HC at 5 V: ±4 mA with guaranteed levels, 25 mA absolute maximum
330 Ω at 5 V ≈ 9 mA, 1 kΩ ≈ 3 mA
slides.notes: A CMOS output acts as a switch with some 10 Ω, so the formula still applies. In the capstone the three encoder bits drive three LEDs to ground, exactly this circuit. Exercise 1.5.

slides.title: Capacitor and RC time constant
bullets: I = C·dV/dt: the voltage cannot jump; at DC a charged C is an open circuit
After τ: 63 %, 3τ: 95 %, 5τ: 99.3 % (settled)
Settling to 1 %: 4.6τ; to ½ LSB of an n-bit ADC: τ·ln(2^{n+1})
Filters and hold capacitors: C0G or film, not X7R/Y5V

falstad.name: rc_charging
falstad.hint: 10 kΩ, 10 µF, τ = 0.1 s: read 3.16 V at 0.1 s on the scope

slides.notes: The 3-bit capstone converter needs 2.8τ, a 12-bit converter 9τ; that is why acquisition time is always given with an accuracy. Exercise 1.6 reads the charging and discharging values from the scope.

slides.title: Preview: the RC low-pass
bullets: Slow signals pass, fast ones are attenuated: −20 dB per decade above f_{c}
At f_{c}: amplitude 0.707 (−3 dB), phase −45°
Capstone anti-aliasing: f_{c} = 2.34 Hz with 6.8 kΩ and 10 µF

falstad.name: rc_lowpass
falstad.hint: 1 kHz sine at f_{c} = 995 Hz: output 0.705 V, lags ≈ ¼ period

slides.notes: The same RC circuit seen in the frequency domain. The chapter Active Filters treats filters in detail. Change the source frequency in Falstad and watch the amplitude.

slides.title: Working with Falstad

left.head: Pitfalls
bullets: Wires connect only at end points
Every circuit needs a ground
Singular matrix: floating node

right.head: Measuring
bullets: Hover: V, I and P bottom right
Right click → View in New Scope
Sliders for the values worth changing

slides.notes: Open falstad.com/circuit/circuitjs.html, import an example via File → Import From Text. Show led_resistor live: hover over VLED and the resistor. Circuits with capacitors need a few time constants before the values settle.
